title: The Seventy Years and the Nature of Prayer
english: He asks: 'Tell me, when do you think that which is in Isaiah will be fulfilled?' 'And it shall be,' he says, 'after seventy years Tyre shall be restored to its ancient state' (Isaiah 39:7). From when of the seventy years are they counted? Not so that I may take them according to history, but seventy cycles of the sun of righteousness, seventy years. For the sun goes around, illuminating souls and making the doctrines of truth manifest and sending forth its rays. Therefore, when anyone is perfected and has reached the end of his progress, then the seventy years are established for him. As for the stated text, the deviation is not appropriate, but as a question, it is necessary.

Listen, O Lord, to my voice, which I have cried out (Psalm 142:1). I cried a voice to You, requesting what it would be good for me to have. And that which is paradoxical: it sends back a prayer of prayer; for he who entreats someone whose prayer has failed, offers a prayer in place of a prayer. Praying, I cried out to You again, beseeching, so that You might listen to this voice, which I cried out to You. For not everyone who cries according to the inner man cries to God, but he who says the things of God, bringing a petition to Him. The Sodomites also cry, but not to God: 'The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has filled [the heavens] and their sins are very great' (Genesis 18:20). And concerning the Ninevites it is said: 'The cry of their wickedness ascended' (Jonah 3:4), the multitude of wickedness. And in Isaiah: 'I waited to do justice, but he made a cry instead' (Isaiah 5:7). Thus, the cry of the Sodomites is an injunction of wickedness.

But he who prays cries to God when he has an uplifted voice, when he prays concerning great things, not concerning trivial and contemptible things, the one requesting that good things might be given to him. And the other Evangelist, the Holy Spirit, interpreted the good things; for writing in the same place, Matthew says: 'He will give good things to those asking Him' (Matthew 7:11), while Luke says: 'He will give the Holy Spirit' (Luke 11:13). The Spirit, being one, is a multitude of good things according to His various gifts; for he who has the Holy Spirit has the gifts of the Spirit, which are many good things. And in essence He is one, but in His thoughts He is many good things, just as God is one in essence. It is said also that He is many according to various thoughts: good, unshakeable, unchangeable, fountain, light; and likewise the Savior is one.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Satiety and the Divine Light
english: That which is called life and truth according to its underlying reality. 'Ask,' he says, 'the great things, and the small things will be added to you.' Thus, the one asking for small things says to God, but not with a shouting voice. 'Ask,' he says, 'the heavenly things, and the earthly things will be added to you.' Therefore, the one sending up a prayer concerning sensible things previously does not cry out to God; he speaks to Him calmly. But the one asking for those truly great and heavenly things and those making one god-like cries out to God. For thought is the cry.

7–8 'Have mercy on me and hear me,' my heart has said to you (Psalm 51:1). My mind has said to you: 'from you I ask mercy.' My heart expects mercy from you and says to you, 'hear me.' These things turn back toward themselves: the one being shown mercy by God is heard, and the one being heard is shown mercy. It is not possible, then, to say one before the other. But to hear precedes to show mercy. Yet not in time before. And just as it is not possible to say appearance before color, nor color before appearance. If there is color, there is appearance. If there is appearance, it has been colored. Appearance is pre-conceived. It is necessary for there to be an appearance, so that there may be such color. And the 'it is necessary' I do not take according to time, but according to thought.

'My heart has said to you.' It signifies persons. According to every word, the three persons are signified: the one speaking, and that toward which he speaks, and that concerning which he speaks. Therefore, the person of the one praying is the one now announcing. And he announces the petition to no one other than God. 8 'I sought your face' (Psalm 27:8). My heart saying, 'have mercy and hear me.' I did not seek your face before now. Your face, I did not entreat only now: 'let your face shine upon me and we shall be saved' (Psalm 27:9). And 'I sought' signifies a seeking that was not raised. 8 'Your face, Lord, I will seek.' My heart, Lord, will seek your face. Even if 'I sought' and I had it grasping me, I do not cease until this. Again I seek it. 9 'Do not turn your face away from me' (Psalm 27:9). The eye which is healthy and preserves the virtue of sight, when light is present, has a desire for it, and it is never satisfied; for light is insatiable for the eyes: 'sweet to the eyes,' as the Preacher says (Psalm 19:8). But no one takes satisfaction from the sweet. There is sweet...

Things that satisfy the child, like the sweetness from honey. But that which comes from the light has no satiety, especially when the vision possesses its own inherent virtue. Therefore, moving from the sensible to the intelligible: the eye of the inner man, or the eyes, are never filled and never receive satiety from the face of God; for it is always appearing, illuminating and increasing the desire. 'The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord' (Ps 4:6); it remains. But that of the sun, or generally of the sensible light, does not remain. For if anyone withdraws from seeing the light or closes the eyes, he does not have it marked. But the intelligible light appears to remain to the one having been illuminated; it is not cast away.

Do not turn away in anger from your servant (Ps 103:13). It is possible for one to seem as if God is turning away, but not in anger. Some thought that He turned away from Job when his possessions, his children, and his body were delivered to the one asking; but this did not happen in anger. May it not happen so concerning me, from our own sluggishness, so that you should turn your face away from me in anger. Both are therefore possible; may such a thing not be done to me, so that having been angered, you turn away from me. Or thus: may you not be angered in such a way that I am deprived of your presence. 'Become my helper, do not cast me off' (Ps 142:5). Some manuscripts have: 'do not forsake me.' To cast off, to reject, to send away, is the same as to cast off. For in Isaiah it is carried: 'and he casts him off' (Isa 17:4). And observe the precision of the word; it does not always mean the occurrence of a becoming, but rather signifies that which the addition intends. And 'become my helper' is applied here. For one who is becoming a helper to someone does not simply 'become.' I have also said at other times that verbs which imply a becoming, if they are spoken unrestrictedly, signify a creative act: 'all things came into being through him,' instead of 'all things came into being through him.' 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth' (Gen 1:1). It is not 'what He made,' but this very thing: 'heaven and earth.' And when it says: 'become my helper, do not forsake me,' it says: 'become a helper to me.' The relationship signifies the helper in relation to the one being helped. So we also say: 'become my teacher,' and it does not mean they are a teacher, but 'become a teacher to me.' Such things are also...

title: The distinction between hating parents and hating God
english: Things said about the Savior: 'Understand the apostle and high priest of our confession, faithful in him who made him' (Hebrews 3:6). He made him an apostle; he did not merely make him, but an apostle. And behold, the essence of the Son is eternal. But to become an apostle happens then, when some depart from him; for he is sent to those far off. And observe that the becoming an apostle co-exists with him being far from certain ones, those having been distanced from him.

Again, he becomes high priest when he is set over those for whom he is consecrated. But it is not then that the hypostasis of the Savior has become, as those think, but the beginning, the high priesthood. Thus also in the deeds of the apostles he says: 'Let all the house of Israel know securely this, that God made him both Lord and Christ' (Acts 20:25). He becomes Lord of those fleeing to serve him. If therefore anyone begins to serve him even today, he has become Lord to him today. And if anyone subjects him to his own kingdom and to his own priesthood, he has become Christ to him today; for the Christ declares nothing other than king and high priest.

Indeed, Aaron was said to be the Lord's Christ, and the kings were said to be the Lord's Christs, and concerning Saul: 'The Lord is a witness, and his Christ' (1 Samuel 24:6). And this: 'Do not touch my Christs.' 'My helper' therefore means 'become, do not lead me astray'; do not send me away from you. Concerning some it is said: 'God will cast them away, because they did not listen to him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations' (Psalm 80:12). When they depart, they were led astray here and there, no longer having a firm purpose. And he assigns the cause to us: 'because they did not listen.' It is not God's will to cast anyone away from him. But it is his will to send away those who did not listen, so that he might not seem to hate virtue. And since they did not listen, 'according to the abundance of their lawlessness, cast them out, because they have turned aside from you, Lord' (Psalm 64:6). This is what it means to be led astray.

And they say also that the word is etymologized such that the iron filings are called the 'koras'. Easily the filings are scattered like dust. May I not become such a thing as to be led astray. I wish to be a vessel of gold or a vessel of bronze, but certainly not the dross.

And [it] is sent away and cast out. 9 And do not leave me, Lord God my Savior. For you are also my Lord—for I serve you—and my God—for I am a child of Abraham, and God is 'of Abraham and of Isaac' (Gen 21:10) and clearly of them—I am as a slave toward a lord, as one worshipping sincerely toward God, being healed, as one being saved toward a Savior. Since therefore all these things have become mine, you do not leave me.

10 For my father and my mother have left me. I wish to clarify this with an explicit evangelical sense, so that it may be understood from that. And the Old Scripture and the Gospel and the very exhortations of the Savior teach to love father and mother. Listen: if anyone hates a father, he does not hate him as a father, but as an impious man; and he hates him not in his capacity as father, but in his capacity as impious. And he who loves a father, does so because of this, that he truly pursues [him] when he is thus trained by fear and instruction, when he is thus trained as a righteous man. 'Well' indeed 'a father trains a righteous man'. I have said therefore that almost all the Scriptures speak against and punish those who fall away from the honor of parents: 'he who slanders a father or mother shall be executed by death'. Therefore listen: 'he who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me'. Even though [it says] 'honor your parents and love father and mother' (Ex 20:12), but when [one does so] above God, he is slandered; for when he is about to confess the truth while being restrained by persecution, and when he says, 'because of the old age of the father and the mother I do not wish to die', and betrays [them], loving the parents above God, he has preferred the disposition toward the parents over the piety toward God. And this is what is slandered.

In the Gospel, indeed, the Savior says: 'Having turned', he says, 'Jesus said to the crowds: If anyone wants to come after me, if he does not hate his father and his mother and his wife and his brothers and his children, he cannot be my disciple' (Luke 14:26). If you have legislated honor concerning parents and promised me great labors saying: 'Honor your father and your mother, so that it may go well with you and you may be long-lived on the earth' (Matt 19:17), how do you now say: 'If someone does not hate father and mother, he cannot follow me'? The hatred here is called differently, the [hatred] not...
